prompt: Why is IPv6 needed?
chosen: Because of IPv4 address exhaustion. IPv4's 32-bit addresses only allow about 4.3 billion unique values, and even fewer are usable for hosts, which isn't enough for the number of connected devices today.
rejected: Because IPv4 is too slow for modern networks. IPv6 packets are processed faster thanks to the larger address space.

prompt: What happened to IPv5?
chosen: Version number 5 was used by Internet Stream Protocol, an experimental protocol family. IPv4's successor was named IPv6 to avoid confusion with it.
rejected: IPv5 was developed but abandoned during testing because it had the same address exhaustion problem as IPv4.

prompt: How long is an IPv6 address?
chosen: 128 bits — four times the length of an IPv4 address.
rejected: 64 bits — twice the length of an IPv4 address.

prompt: Does IPv6 provide four times as many addresses as IPv4?
chosen: No. Each extra bit doubles the total, so going from 32 to 128 bits gives vastly more — about 340 undecillion addresses rather than four times 4.3 billion.
rejected: Yes. IPv6 addresses are four times longer, so the address space is exactly four times larger.

prompt: What is IANA?
chosen: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, which controls IP address assignments. It distributes address space to the Regional Internet Registries.
rejected: The International Association of Network Administrators, which publishes the standards that define IP addressing.

prompt: What is an RIR?
chosen: A Regional Internet Registry. There are five, each serving a different part of the world, and they assign addresses to organisations such as ISPs.
rejected: A Reserved IP Range, meaning a block of addresses set aside for private or experimental use.

prompt: What is a nibble?
chosen: A group of four bits — half a byte. One hexadecimal digit represents exactly one nibble.
rejected: A group of two bits, which is the smallest unit hexadecimal can represent.

prompt: Why does one hexadecimal digit represent four bits?
chosen: Because hexadecimal has 16 digits and 2^4 = 16, so four bits cover exactly the range 0 to F.
rejected: Because hexadecimal is base 16 and 16 divided by 4 gives the number of bits each digit holds.

prompt: How do you convert a binary number to hexadecimal?
chosen: Split it into four-bit groups, convert each group to decimal, then convert each decimal value to its hexadecimal digit.
rejected: Split it into eight-bit groups, convert each to decimal, then write each decimal value in hexadecimal.

prompt: What is hexadecimal D in decimal?
How big is the IPv6 header?
chosen: A fixed 40 bytes. Unlike IPv4, whose header varies from 20 to 60 bytes, IPv6's is always the same size.
rejected: It varies from 40 to 80 bytes depending on whether extension headers are present.

prompt: How many fields does the IPv6 header have?
chosen: Eight: Version, Traffic Class, Flow Label, Payload Length, Next Header, Hop Limit, Source Address, and Destination Address.
rejected: Fourteen, the same as the IPv4 header, though several have been renamed.

prompt: Why does IPv6 need only one length field where IPv4 needs two?
chosen: Because the IPv6 header is a fixed 40 bytes, so there is no need for a header length field. Payload Length alone is enough.
rejected: Because IPv6 packets cannot be fragmented, so the total length never changes in transit.

prompt: What is the IPv6 Next Header field equivalent to in IPv4?
chosen: The Protocol field. It indicates what kind of message is encapsulated in the packet.
rejected: The Internet Header Length field, since it tells the receiver where the next part of the packet begins.

prompt: What is the Hop Limit field equivalent to in IPv4?
chosen: The Time to Live field. Each router decrements it by 1, and the packet is dropped if it reaches 0.
rejected: The Fragment Offset field, which tracks how far the packet has travelled through the network.

prompt: What Next Header value indicates ICMPv6?
rejected: 1, the same value IPv4 uses for ICMP.

prompt: How is an IPv6 address written?
chosen: As eight groups of 16 bits, separated by colons, with each group written in hexadecimal.
rejected: As sixteen groups of 8 bits, separated by colons, with each group written in hexadecimal.

prompt: What is a hextet?
chosen: The informal term for each group of 16 bits in an IPv6 address. There is no official term — the precise word would be hexadectet.
rejected: The official term for each group of 6 bits in an IPv6 address, as defined by the IPv6 standard.

prompt: What prefix length do IPv6 networks typically use?
chosen: /64. It is hugely inefficient — each subnet holds about 18 quintillion addresses — but the address space is so large that the simplicity is worth it.
rejected: /48, which is the block size assigned to an enterprise by its ISP.

prompt: How are IPv6 prefix lengths written?
chosen: Always with slash notation, such as /64. There are no dotted-decimal netmasks in IPv6.
rejected: Either with slash notation or with a hexadecimal netmask, depending on the command being used.

prompt: What are the two ways to abbreviate an IPv6 address?
chosen: Remove leading zeros from each hextet, and replace two or more consecutive all-zero hextets with a double colon.
rejected: Remove trailing zeros from each hextet, and replace any single all-zero hextet with a double colon.

prompt: Can you remove trailing zeros from a hextet?
chosen: No, only leading zeros. So 0020 becomes 20, but 2000 stays as 2000.
rejected: Yes. Zeros can be removed from either end of a hextet as long as at least one digit remains.

prompt: How do you abbreviate the hextet 0000?
chosen: As a single 0. You can remove three of the four zeros but not all four.
rejected: You remove it entirely, leaving two consecutive colons in its place.

prompt: How many times can a double colon appear in an IPv6 address?
chosen: Only once. If there are two separate runs of all-zero hextets, only one of them can be abbreviated that way.
rejected: Twice, as long as the two runs are separated by at least one non-zero hextet so there is no ambiguity.

prompt: Can a single all-zero hextet be replaced with a double colon?
chosen: No. The double colon requires two or more consecutive all-zero hextets.
rejected: Yes. Any all-zero hextet can be replaced, which is why 2001:db8::1:2:3:4:5 is valid.

prompt: If an address has two runs of all-zero hextets of different lengths, which gets abbreviated?
chosen: The longest one. If they are the same length, you abbreviate the leftmost.
rejected: The leftmost one, regardless of length, since that keeps the address easiest to read.

prompt: Should IPv6 addresses use uppercase or lowercase hex letters?
chosen: Lowercase, according to RFC 5952. Cisco IOS show commands display them in uppercase anyway, since RFC 5952 isn't a full standard.
rejected: Uppercase, which is why Cisco IOS displays them that way in all its output.

prompt: How do you find the prefix of the address 2001:db8:1:2:a:b:c:d/64?
chosen: Set the host portion to zero. With a /64 that means zeroing the last four hextets, giving 2001:db8:1:2::/64.
rejected: Set the first four hextets to zero, giving ::a:b:c:d/64, since the prefix identifies the host portion.

prompt: What command enables IPv6 routing on a Cisco router?
chosen: ipv6 unicast-routing, in global configuration mode. Without it the router can hold IPv6 addresses but won't forward IPv6 packets.
rejected: ipv6 routing, in global configuration mode. IPv6 forwarding is otherwise enabled by default like IPv4.

prompt: Is IPv6 routing enabled by default on a Cisco router?
chosen: No. IPv4 routing is enabled by default but IPv6 routing is not — it is easy to forget.
rejected: Yes, as long as at least one interface has an IPv6 address configured.

prompt: What command assigns an IPv6 address to an interface?
chosen: ipv6 address, followed by the address and prefix length in slash notation.
rejected: ipv6 address, followed by the address and then a separate hexadecimal netmask.

prompt: What happens if you configure a second IPv4 address on an interface?
chosen: It overwrites the first one. Only the most recently configured address remains, unless you add the secondary keyword.
rejected: Both addresses are kept, and the interface responds on either of them.

prompt: What happens if you configure a second IPv6 address on an interface?
chosen: Both are kept. Unlike IPv4, IPv6 addresses don't overwrite each other, so you must use the no command to remove one.
rejected: The second overwrites the first, exactly as it does with IPv4 addresses.

prompt: What is Modified EUI-64?
chosen: A method of automatically generating the 64-bit interface identifier — the host portion of an IPv6 address — from the interface's 48-bit MAC address.
rejected: A method of compressing a 64-bit IPv6 prefix into a shorter form for easier configuration.

prompt: What are the three steps of Modified EUI-64?
chosen: Divide the MAC address in half, insert fffe in the middle to reach 64 bits, then invert the seventh bit.
rejected: Divide the MAC address in half, insert ffff in the middle, then invert the first bit.

prompt: Which bit does Modified EUI-64 invert, and where is it?
chosen: The seventh bit, which is the third bit of the second hexadecimal digit.
rejected: The seventh bit, which is the third bit of the seventh hexadecimal digit.

prompt: How do you configure an address using Modified EUI-64?
chosen: Specify a /64 prefix in the ipv6 address command and add the eui-64 keyword at the end.
rejected: Use the ipv6 eui-64 command in interface config mode and let the router pick the prefix automatically.

prompt: What does the Modified in Modified EUI-64 refer to?
chosen: The inversion of the seventh bit. Plain EUI-64 would just insert fffe without flipping that bit.
rejected: The insertion of fffe, which modifies the original 48-bit MAC address into a 64-bit value.

prompt: What are the five main IPv6 address types?
chosen: Global unicast, unique local, link-local, multicast, and anycast.
rejected: Global unicast, unique local, link-local, multicast, and broadcast.

prompt: What is a global unicast address?
chosen: A globally unique IPv6 address used for communication over the public internet. Allocation is controlled by IANA and distributed through the RIRs and ISPs.
rejected: An address that can reach any host globally, including those using private addressing, by being routed through a translation gateway.

prompt: What range were global unicast addresses originally defined as?
chosen: 2000::/3, covering 2000:: through 3fff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff. The definition has since widened to include anything not reserved for another purpose.
rejected: 2001::/16, which is why most public IPv6 addresses seen today begin with 2001.

prompt: What are the three parts of a global unicast address?
chosen: A 48-bit global routing prefix assigned by the ISP or RIR, a 16-bit subnet identifier the enterprise uses to create subnets, and a 64-bit interface identifier.
rejected: A 64-bit global routing prefix, a 32-bit subnet identifier, and a 32-bit interface identifier.

prompt: What is the IPv4 equivalent of a global unicast address?
chosen: A public IPv4 address — any address not in a reserved private or special-purpose range.
rejected: A class A address, which is the range originally reserved for large organisations connecting to the internet.

prompt: What range is reserved for documentation examples?
rejected: 2000::/3, which is why textbook examples always begin with 2000.

prompt: What is a unique local address?
chosen: A private IPv6 address. It doesn't have to be globally unique and can be used freely inside an enterprise, but it can't be used over the internet — ISPs drop packets using them.
rejected: An address that is guaranteed unique worldwide but is only routed within the local organisation.

prompt: What range are IPv6 unique local addresses in?
chosen: fc00::/7, but that splits into fc00::/8 which is reserved, and fd00::/8 which is the active range. So ULAs in practice begin with fd.
rejected: fe80::/10, with the first 54 bits following it set to zero.

prompt: What are the three private IPv4 ranges?
Why should a ULA's global ID be randomly generated?
chosen: To make overlap between organisations unlikely. If two companies merge and need to integrate their networks, random global IDs mean their addresses almost certainly won't clash.
rejected: Because the standard requires ULAs to be globally unique, so random generation is the only way to guarantee that.

prompt: What is a link-local address?
chosen: A unicast address that can only be used for communication between devices on the same link or segment. Devices on different segments cannot communicate using them.
rejected: An address that identifies the physical link itself rather than any particular device on it.

prompt: What range do IPv6 link-local addresses use?
chosen: fe80::/10, but the standard requires the next 54 bits to be zero, so in practice every LLA uses the fe80::/64 prefix.
rejected: fe80::/64 exactly, with no larger range defined.

prompt: How does an interface get its link-local address?
chosen: It is generated automatically using Modified EUI-64 as soon as IPv6 is enabled on the interface. You can also configure one manually.
rejected: It must be manually configured. Unlike global unicast addresses, LLAs are never generated automatically.

prompt: How many link-local addresses can an interface have?
chosen: Exactly one. Configuring a new one overwrites the old, which differs from global unicast and unique local addresses that accumulate.
rejected: As many as you configure. Like other IPv6 address types, LLAs do not overwrite each other.

prompt: What command enables IPv6 on an interface without giving it an address?
chosen: ipv6 enable. The interface then has only its automatically generated link-local address.
rejected: ipv6 unicast-routing, applied in interface configuration mode.

prompt: How do you manually set a link-local address?
chosen: Use ipv6 address followed by the address and the link-local keyword. No prefix length is specified.
rejected: Use ipv6 address followed by the address and /64, the same as any other IPv6 address.

prompt: What is the IPv4 equivalent of the link-local range?
chosen: 169.254.0.0/16. The key difference is that IPv6 requires every enabled interface to have an LLA, while IPv4 does not.
rejected: 127.0.0.0/8, which is reserved for local communication that doesn't leave the device.

prompt: What range do IPv6 multicast addresses use?
chosen: ff00::/8. If an address begins with ff, it is a multicast address.
rejected: fe00::/8, which distinguishes them from the fe80::/10 link-local range.

prompt: What are the IPv6 multicast scopes?
chosen: Interface-local (ff01), link-local (ff02), site-local (ff05), organization-local (ff08), and global (ff0e).
rejected: Interface-local (ff01), link-local (ff02), area-local (ff03), site-local (ff04), and global (ff05).

prompt: What does the link-local multicast scope mean?
chosen: The packet stays on the local segment — routers will not forward it.
rejected: The packet is sent only to devices with link-local addresses, ignoring those with global unicast addresses.

prompt: What is the IPv6 all-nodes multicast address?
chosen: ff02::1. The IPv4 equivalent is 224.0.0.1.
rejected: ff02::2. The IPv4 equivalent is 224.0.0.1.

prompt: What is the IPv6 all-routers multicast address?
What IPv6 multicast address do all OSPF routers use?
chosen: ff02::5, matching IPv4's 224.0.0.5.
rejected: ff02::6, matching IPv4's 224.0.0.5.

prompt: What IPv6 multicast address do all EIGRP routers use?
chosen: ff02::a, matching IPv4's 224.0.0.10. Remember that hexadecimal a equals decimal 10.
rejected: ff02::10, matching IPv4's 224.0.0.10 exactly.

prompt: Does IPv6 have broadcast addresses?
chosen: No. IPv6 has no broadcast. Instead hosts use the all-nodes multicast address ff02::1, which reaches every host on the segment and achieves the same effect.
rejected: Yes, but the broadcast address is written as ffff:: rather than as all ones like in IPv4.

prompt: What command shows which multicast groups an interface has joined?
chosen: show ipv6 interface, optionally with the interface name.
rejected: show ipv6 multicast groups.

prompt: What is anycast?
chosen: One-to-one-of-multiple communication. The same address is configured on several hosts, and packets are delivered to whichever one is nearest according to the routers along the path.
rejected: One-to-multiple communication where a packet is copied and delivered to every host sharing the address.

prompt: Is there a reserved range for anycast addresses?
chosen: No. An anycast address is indistinguishable from an ordinary unicast address — it just happens to be configured on more than one host.
rejected: Yes, the fc00::/7 range is shared between unique local and anycast addresses.

prompt: Why is anycast useful for internet services?
chosen: The same address can be configured on servers in different parts of the world, so each user reaches the closest one. That lowers latency, which is why CDNs use it.
rejected: It lets a single server handle more connections by distributing them across multiple network interfaces.

prompt: What does the anycast keyword do in the ipv6 address command?
chosen: It marks the address as anycast in some show command output, shown as [ANY]. It doesn't change the router's behaviour — it just documents the intent.
rejected: It tells the router to advertise the address in a way that allows other routers to select the nearest instance.

prompt: What is the unspecified IPv6 address?
chosen: The all-zeros address, written as ::. It is used as a source address when a device doesn't yet know its own IPv6 address, and in default routes as ::/0. The IPv4 equivalent is 0.0.0.0.
rejected: The address ::1, used when a device has not yet been assigned an address by DHCP.

prompt: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
chosen: ::1. Messages sent to it are looped back to the local device without leaving any interface. The IPv4 equivalent is the 127.0.0.0/8 range.
rejected: ::0, which is the first address in the reserved loopback block.

prompt: What are the four communication methods in IPv6?
chosen: Unicast is one-to-one, multicast is one-to-multiple, and anycast is one-to-one-of-multiple. IPv6 has no broadcast.
rejected: Unicast is one-to-one, broadcast is one-to-all, multicast is one-to-multiple, and anycast is one-to-one-of-multiple.
